title: India's Parliament Just Opened a Net Neutrality Inquiry Over Airtel's New Premium 5G Plan. Meta, Google, X, and Amazon Have Been Summoned.
excerpt: The standing committee wants to know what happens to 90 percent of India's mobile users — all on prepaid — when telecom companies start selling faster internet to those who pay more
body:
India's Parliament has opened a formal inquiry into whether Bharti Airtel's new Priority Postpaid plan — the country's first commercial 5G network slicing product — violates the principle that every internet user deserves equal access.

The Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, chaired by BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, on Tuesday directed the Department of Telecommunications and the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India to study the impact of 5G network slicing services in countries like Singapore and the United Kingdom. The committee also decided to summon Meta, X, Google, and Amazon to discuss net neutrality and preferential access practices.

## What Is Airtel Priority?

Airtel Priority Postpaid is India's first consumer-facing product built on 5G network slicing, a technology that allows a telecom operator to carve a single physical network into multiple virtual networks, each tuned for different performance profiles. One slice might deliver ultra-low latency for gaming; another might guarantee bandwidth for video calls; a third might be optimized for massive IoT deployments.

In practice, Airtel's Priority plan promises enhanced network capabilities — faster speeds, lower latency, priority routing during congestion — exclusively to its postpaid subscribers who pay a premium. In a communication to users, Airtel said the technology had already been deployed in several Western markets.

## Why Parliament Is Concerned

The issue is deceptively simple: if a telecom company can sell better internet to people who pay more, what happens to everyone else?

In India, that question hits harder than in most countries. Nearly 90 percent of Indian mobile subscribers are on prepaid plans — the cheapest way to stay connected in a country where per-capita income is roughly $2,700. The committee flagged this explicitly.

"Nearly 90 per cent users are having prepaid mobile connections. How can their rights be bypassed?" a person familiar with the committee discussions said. "DoT and TRAI have been asked to give a detailed response."

India's net neutrality framework, established in 2017 after a landmark campaign that defeated Facebook's Free Basics initiative, prohibits internet service providers from blocking, degrading, or slowing content. But it was written before 5G network slicing existed as a commercial product, and the regulatory language does not explicitly address the practice of offering differentiated quality of service tiers on the same network.

## The Global Precedent

The committee's decision to study Singapore and UK implementations is significant. Both countries have permitted some form of 5G network slicing, but under different regulatory frameworks. Singapore's approach has been relatively permissive, while UK regulators have imposed guardrails to ensure that base-tier service does not degrade as premium tiers expand.

The distinction matters. If slicing simply adds a premium tier without degrading the standard experience, it looks more like a first-class airline cabin than a toll road. If the premium tier comes at the expense of base service, it looks like a two-tier internet — exactly what net neutrality was designed to prevent.

## What Comes Next

After Tuesday's meeting, Dubey struck a measured tone. "We have to look after 140 crore people. All of them should get equal rights. Right of Equality," he said, while clarifying that the committee had reached no conclusions yet.

The summoning of Meta, X, Google, and Amazon signals that the inquiry may extend beyond telecom into broader questions of platform-level preferential access — whether social media companies boost paying users in algorithmic ranking, or whether cloud platforms offer tiered service that disadvantages smaller businesses.

For India's tech ecosystem, the stakes are real. Startups building on mobile-first infrastructure could find themselves competing not just on product quality but on network access. If Airtel's premium slicing takes off and Jio and Vi follow suit, the base layer of the Indian internet — the one that 90 percent of users rely on — will be defined by whatever is left after the premium customers are served.

The committee has asked DoT and TRAI to report back in the coming weeks. The answer will shape how 1.4 billion people experience the internet.
author: Diaspora Desk
